titre: Ultramarine, the Blue That Cost More Than Gold
accroche: In an old master painting, the blue of the Virgin's cloak is not a theological choice: it is a line item, pricier than gold by weight.
contenu_vulgarise:
In the sixteenth century, a patron negotiating the price of a religious painting does not only discuss the composition or the number of figures: he also negotiates, line by line, how much of a certain blue the painter may use. This blue, ultramarine, is made from lapis lazuli, a semi-precious stone imported almost exclusively from the mines of Badakhshan, in present-day Afghanistan, the same deposits worked since antiquity.

## The price of a color

Extracting a pure pigment from the raw stone, full of white calcite and golden pyrite, requires a long purification process: the ground lapis lazuli is kneaded into a paste of wax and resin, then washed several times, each wash yielding a slightly less pure grade of blue than the one before. The most concentrated result, reserved for the most prestigious uses, at times becomes costlier than gold by the same weight: a 2020 study by the Rijksmuseum, the University of Amsterdam, VU Amsterdam, and the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility in Grenoble, published in the journal *Science Advances*, confirmed that by the seventeenth century ultramarine indeed exceeded the price of gold. The same study, using X-ray analysis of old-master paint samples, discovered that painters often heated the raw lapis lazuli stone red-hot before grinding it, a step that improved the pigment's yield and that no written source had ever mentioned: a workshop practice invisible for four centuries, until physics found it again.

This cost explains why Renaissance commission contracts so often specify, beyond the price of labor, the quality and quantity of ultramarine the painter may use: some patrons even buy the pigment themselves and supply it directly to the workshop, rather than let the painter set its price. Painters then reserve a cheaper blue, azurite, for skies and minor figures, keeping ultramarine for what matters most.

## A blue that shows its price

This economics sheds light on a convention usually read as purely religious: why, in so many old paintings, does the Virgin Mary wear the most intensely blue cloak in the whole scene, more so than any other figure. Ultramarine is used above all to mark the most important figures in a composition, and none is more important than the mother of Christ. Dressing the Virgin in the most expensive pigment available is therefore not just a theological choice: it is also a way, for the patron paying for that color separately in his contract, to display both his wealth and his piety in the same place, as legible to a fifteenth-century eye as a price tag.

carte.punch: The blue of the Virgin's cloak is often the priciest line in the painter's contract.
carte.idee: Made from Afghan lapis lazuli, the pigment ultramarine cost more than gold by weight in the seventeenth century. Patrons fixed its quantity in the painter's contract and reserved it for the most important figures, which is why the Virgin's cloak is so intensely blue.

quiz.question: Why is the blue of the Virgin Mary's cloak so often the most intense in old paintings?
choix: Because ultramarine cost more than gold, and reserving it for the Virgin displayed the patron's wealth and piety
Because blue was the only color painters could make without risk of fading over time
Because a rule of the Church required this exact color for the Virgin, under penalty of sanction
Because painting workshops had an unlimited supply of this color, unlike other pigments
quiz.explication: Ultramarine, made from lapis lazuli, cost more than gold by weight: reserving it for the Virgin displayed both her central place in the scene and the wealth, and therefore the piety, of the patron who paid for this pigment separately in the contract. Nothing suggests a Church rule or an unlimited supply.
